<span class="atom-split" data-atom="nicholas_nickleby" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby" data-chapter="" data-kind="intro"></span>


THE LIFE AND ADVENTURES OF [[characters/nicholas-nickleby|NICHOLAS NICKLEBY]],

containing a Faithful Account of the Fortunes, Misfortunes,

Uprisings, Downfallings and Complete Career of the Nickelby Family


by Charles Dickens




AUTHOR’S PREFACE


This story was begun, within a few months after the publication of
the completed “[[works/pickwick-(chesterton)|Pickwick]] Papers.” There were, then, a good many cheap
Yorkshire schools in existence. There are very few now.

Of the monstrous neglect of [[concepts/education|education]] in England, and the disregard
of it by the State as a means of forming good or bad citizens, and
miserable or happy men, private schools long afforded a notable example.
Although any man who had proved his unfitness for any other occupation
in life, was free, without examination or qualification, to open a
school anywhere; although preparation for the functions he undertook,
was required in the surgeon who assisted to bring a boy into the world,
or might one day assist, perhaps, to send him out of it; in the chemist,
the attorney, the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker; the whole
round of crafts and trades, the schoolmaster excepted; and although
schoolmasters, as a race, were the blockheads and impostors who might
naturally be expected to [[motifs/spring|spring]] from such a state of things, and to
flourish in it; these Yorkshire schoolmasters were the lowest and most
rotten round in the whole ladder. Traders in the avarice, indifference,
or imbecility of parents, and the helplessness of children; ignorant,
sordid, brutal men, to whom few considerate persons would have entrusted
the board and lodging of a [[motifs/horse|horse]] or a dog; they formed the worthy
cornerstone of a structure, which, for absurdity and a magnificent
high-minded LAISSEZ-ALLER neglect, has rarely been exceeded in the
world.

We hear sometimes of an action for damages against the unqualified
medical practitioner, who has deformed a broken limb in pretending to
heal it. But, what of the hundreds of thousands of minds that have been
deformed for ever by the incapable pettifoggers who have pretended to
form them!

I make mention of the race, as of the Yorkshire schoolmasters, in the
past tense. Though it has not yet finally disappeared, it is dwindling
daily. A long day’s work remains to be done about us in the way of
[[concepts/education|education]], Heaven knows; but great improvements and facilities towards
the attainment of a good one, have been furnished, of late years.

I cannot call to mind, now, how I came to hear about Yorkshire schools
when I was a not very robust [[archetypes/child|child]], sitting in bye-places near Rochester
[[settings/castle|Castle]], with a head full of PARTRIDGE, STRAP, TOM PIPES, and SANCHO
PANZA; but I know that my first impressions of them were picked up
at that [[motifs/time|time]], and that they were somehow or other connected with a
suppurated abscess that some boy had come [[motifs/home|home]] with, in consequence of
his Yorkshire guide, philosopher, and friend, having ripped it open with
an inky pen-knife. The impression made upon me, however made, never left
me. I was always curious about Yorkshire schools--fell, long afterwards
and at sundry times, into the way of hearing more about them--at last,
having an audience, resolved to write about them.

With that intent I went down into Yorkshire before I began this book, in
very severe [[motifs/winter|winter]] [[motifs/time|time]] which is pretty faithfully described herein.
As I wanted to see a schoolmaster or two, and was forewarned that those
gentlemen might, in their modesty, be shy of receiving a visit from the
author of the “[[works/pickwick-(chesterton)|Pickwick]] Papers,” I consulted with a professional friend
who had a Yorkshire connexion, and with whom I concerted a pious fraud.
He gave me some letters of introduction, in the name, I think, of my
travelling companion; they bore reference to a supposititious little boy
who had been left with a widowed mother who didn’t know what to do
with him; the poor lady had thought, as a means of thawing the tardy
compassion of her relations in his behalf, of sending him to a Yorkshire
school; I was the poor lady’s friend, travelling that way; and if
the recipient of the letter could inform me of a school in his
neighbourhood, the writer would be very much obliged.

I went to several places in that part of the country where I understood
the schools to be most plentifully sprinkled, and had no occasion to
deliver a letter until I came to a certain town which shall be nameless.
The person to whom it was addressed, was not at [[motifs/home|home]]; but he came down
at [[motifs/night|night]], through the [[motifs/snow|snow]], to the inn where I was staying. It was after
dinner; and he needed little persuasion to sit down by the [[motifs/fire|fire]] in a
warm corner, and take his share of the wine that was on the table.

I am afraid he is dead now. I recollect he was a jovial, ruddy,
broad-faced man; that we got acquainted directly; and that we talked
on all kinds of subjects, except the school, which he showed a great
anxiety to avoid. “Was there any large school near?” I asked him, in
reference to the letter. “Oh yes,” he said; “there was a pratty big
‘un.” “Was it a good one?” I asked. “Ey!” he said, “it was as good as
anoother; that was a’ a matther of opinion”; and fell to looking at the
[[motifs/fire|fire]], staring round the room, and whistling a little. On my reverting to
some other topic that we had been discussing, he recovered immediately;
but, though I tried him again and again, I never approached the question
of the school, even if he were in the middle of a laugh, without
observing that his countenance fell, and that he became uncomfortable.
At last, when we had passed a couple of hours or so, very agreeably, he
suddenly took up his hat, and leaning over the table and looking me
full in the face, said, in a low voice: “Weel, Misther, we’ve been vara
pleasant toogather, and ar’ll spak’ my moind tiv’ee. Dinnot let the
weedur send her lattle boy to yan o’ our school-measthers, while there’s
a harse to hoold in a’ Lunnun, or a gootther to lie asleep in. Ar
wouldn’t mak’ ill words amang my neeburs, and ar speak tiv’ee quiet
loike. But I’m dom’d if ar can gang to bed and not tellee, for weedur’s
sak’, to keep the lattle boy from a’ sike scoondrels while there’s a
harse to hoold in a’ Lunnun, or a gootther to lie asleep in!” Repeating
these words with great heartiness, and with a solemnity on his jolly
face that made it look twice as large as before, he shook hands and went
away. I never saw him afterwards, but I sometimes imagine that I descry
a faint reflection of him in John Browdie.

In reference to these gentry, I may here quote a few words from the
original preface to this book.

“It has afforded the Author great amusement and satisfaction, during the
progress of this work, to learn, from country friends and from a variety
of ludicrous statements concerning himself in provincial newspapers,
that more than one Yorkshire schoolmaster lays claim to being the
original of Mr. Squeers. One worthy, he has reason to believe, has
actually consulted authorities learned in the law, as to his having good
grounds on which to rest an action for libel; another, has meditated a
[[motifs/journey|journey]] to [[settings/london|London]], for the express purpose of committing an assault and
battery on his traducer; a third, perfectly remembers being waited on,
last January twelve-month, by two gentlemen, one of whom held him
in conversation while the other took his likeness; and, although Mr.
Squeers has but one eye, and he has two, and the published [[forms/sketch|sketch]] does
not resemble him (whoever he may be) in any other respect, still he
and all his friends and neighbours know at once for whom it is meant,
because--the character is SO like him.

“While the Author cannot but feel the full force of the compliment thus
conveyed to him, he ventures to suggest that these contentions may arise
from the fact, that Mr. Squeers is the representative of a class, and
not of an individual. Where imposture, ignorance, and brutal cupidity,
are the stock in trade of a small [[concepts/body|body]] of men, and one is described
by these characteristics, all his fellows will recognise something
belonging to themselves, and each will have a misgiving that the
portrait is his own.

“The Author’s object in calling public attention to the system would be
very imperfectly fulfilled, if he did not state now, in his own person,
emphatically and earnestly, that Mr. Squeers and his school are faint
and feeble pictures of an existing reality, purposely subdued and kept
down lest they should be deemed impossible. That there are, upon record,
trials at law in which damages have been sought as a poor recompense
for lasting agonies and disfigurements inflicted upon children by the
treatment of the master in these places, involving such offensive and
foul details of neglect, cruelty, and disease, as no writer of fiction
would have the boldness to imagine. And that, since he has been engaged
upon these Adventures, he has received, from private quarters far beyond
the reach of suspicion or distrust, accounts of atrocities, in the
perpetration of which upon neglected or repudiated children, these
schools have been the main instruments, very far exceeding any that
appear in these pages.”

This comprises all I need say on the subject; except that if I had seen
occasion, I had resolved to reprint a few of these details of legal
proceedings, from certain old newspapers.

One other quotation from the same Preface may serve to introduce a fact
that my readers may think curious.

“To turn to a more pleasant subject, it may be right to say, that
there ARE two characters in this book which are drawn from life. It is
remarkable that what we call the world, which is so very credulous in
what professes to be true, is most incredulous in what professes to be
imaginary; and that, while, every day in real life, it will allow in one
man no blemishes, and in another no virtues, it will seldom admit a
very strongly-marked character, either good or bad, in a fictitious
narrative, to be within the limits of probability. But those who take an
interest in this tale, will be glad to learn that the BROTHERS CHEERYBLE
live; that their liberal [[concepts/charity|charity]], their singleness of heart, their
noble [[concepts/nature|nature]], and their unbounded benevolence, are no creations of the
Author’s brain; but are prompting every day (and oftenest by stealth)
some munificent and generous deed in that town of which they are the
[[concepts/pride|pride]] and [[concepts/honour|honour]].”

If I were to attempt to sum up the thousands of letters, from all sorts
of people in all sorts of latitudes and climates, which this unlucky
paragraph brought down upon me, I should get into an arithmetical
difficulty from which I could not easily extricate myself. Suffice it
to say, that I believe the applications for loans, gifts, and offices
of profit that I have been requested to forward to the originals of the
BROTHERS CHEERYBLE (with whom I never interchanged any communication
in my life) would have exhausted the combined patronage of all the Lord
Chancellors since the accession of the House of Brunswick, and would
have broken the Rest of the Bank of England.

The Brothers are now dead.

There is only one other point, on which I would [[motifs/desire|desire]] to offer a
remark. If Nicholas be not always found to be blameless or agreeable, he
is not always intended to appear so. He is a young man of an impetuous
temper and of little or no experience; and I saw no reason why such a
[[archetypes/hero|hero]] should be lifted out of [[concepts/nature|nature]].



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_01" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby — Chapter 1 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/memory,motif/well,concept/poverty,form/satire,setting/court,setting/london,character/nicholas_nickleby,character/ralph_nickleby"></span>


CHAPTER 1

Introduces all the Rest


There once lived, in a sequestered part of the county of Devonshire, one
Mr. Godfrey Nickleby: a worthy gentleman, who, taking it into his head
rather late in life that he must get married, and not being young enough
or rich enough to aspire to the hand of a lady of fortune, had wedded an
old flame out of mere attachment, who in her turn had taken him for the
same reason. Thus two people who cannot afford to play cards for money,
sometimes sit down to a quiet game for [[motifs/love|love]].

Some ill-conditioned persons who sneer at the life-matrimonial, may
perhaps suggest, in this place, that the good couple would be better
likened to two principals in a sparring match, who, when fortune is low
and backers scarce, will chivalrously set to, for the mere pleasure
of the buffeting; and in one respect indeed this comparison would hold
good; for, as the adventurous pair of the Fives’ [[settings/court|Court]] will afterwards
send round a hat, and trust to the bounty of the lookers-on for the
means of regaling themselves, so Mr. Godfrey Nickleby and HIS partner,
the honeymoon being over, looked out wistfully into the world, relying
in no inconsiderable degree upon chance for the improvement of their
means. Mr. Nickleby’s income, at the period of his [[motifs/marriage|marriage]], fluctuated
between sixty and eighty pounds PER ANNUM.

There are people enough in the world, Heaven knows! and even in [[settings/london|London]]
(where Mr. Nickleby dwelt in those days) but few complaints prevail, of
the population being scanty. It is extraordinary how long a man may look
among the crowd without discovering the face of a friend, but it is no
less true. Mr. Nickleby looked, and looked, till his eyes became sore
as his heart, but no friend appeared; and when, growing tired of the
search, he turned his eyes homeward, he saw very little there to relieve
his weary vision. A painter who has gazed too long upon some glaring
colour, refreshes his dazzled sight by looking upon a darker and more
sombre tint; but everything that met Mr. Nickleby’s gaze wore so black
and gloomy a hue, that he would have been beyond description refreshed
by the very reverse of the contrast.

At length, after five years, when Mrs. Nickleby had presented her husband
with a couple of sons, and that embarrassed gentleman, impressed with
the necessity of making some provision for his family, was seriously
revolving in his mind a little commercial speculation of insuring his
life next quarter-day, and then falling from the top of the Monument by
accident, there came, one morning, by the general post, a black-bordered
letter to inform him how his uncle, Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], was dead, and
had left him the bulk of his little property, amounting in all to five
thousand pounds sterling.

As the deceased had taken no further notice of his nephew in his
lifetime, than sending to his eldest boy (who had been christened after
him, on desperate speculation) a silver spoon in a morocco case, which,
as he had not too much to eat with it, seemed a kind of [[forms/satire|satire]] upon his
having been born without that useful article of plate in his mouth,
Mr. Godfrey Nickleby could, at first, scarcely believe the tidings thus
conveyed to him. On examination, however, they turned out to be strictly
correct. The amiable old gentleman, it seemed, had intended to leave
the whole to the Royal Humane Society, and had indeed executed a will to
that effect; but the Institution, having been unfortunate enough, a few
months before, to save the life of a poor relation to whom he paid a
weekly allowance of three shillings and sixpence, he had, in a fit of
very natural exasperation, revoked the bequest in a codicil, and left it
all to Mr. Godfrey Nickleby; with a special mention of his indignation,
not only against the society for saving the poor relation’s life, but
against the poor relation also, for allowing himself to be saved.

With a portion of this property Mr. Godfrey Nickleby purchased a small
farm, near Dawlish in Devonshire, whither he retired with his wife and
two children, to live upon the best interest he could get for the rest
of his money, and the little produce he could raise from his land. The
two prospered so [[motifs/well|well]] together that, when he died, some fifteen years
after this period, and some five after his wife, he was enabled to
leave, to his eldest son, Ralph, three thousand pounds in cash, and
to his youngest son, Nicholas, one thousand and the farm, which was as
small a landed estate as one would [[motifs/desire|desire]] to see.

These two brothers had been brought up together in a school at Exeter;
and, being accustomed to go [[motifs/home|home]] once a week, had often heard, from
their mother’s lips, long accounts of their father’s sufferings in his
days of [[concepts/poverty|poverty]], and of their deceased uncle’s importance in his days
of affluence: which recitals produced a very different impression on
the two: for, while the younger, who was of a timid and retiring
disposition, gleaned from thence nothing but forewarnings to shun the
great world and attach himself to the quiet routine of a country life,
Ralph, the elder, deduced from the often-repeated tale the two great
morals that riches are the only true source of happiness and power, and
that it is lawful and just to compass their acquisition by all means
short of felony. ‘And,’ reasoned Ralph with himself, ‘if no good came
of my uncle’s money when he was alive, a great deal of good came of it
after he was dead, inasmuch as my father has got it now, and is saving
it up for me, which is a highly virtuous purpose; and, going back to the
old gentleman, good DID come of it to him too, for he had the pleasure
of thinking of it all his life long, and of being envied and courted
by all his family besides.’ And Ralph always wound up these mental
soliloquies by arriving at the conclusion, that there was nothing like
money.

Not confining himself to theory, or permitting his faculties to rust,
even at that early age, in mere abstract speculations, this promising
lad commenced usurer on a limited scale at school; putting out at good
interest a small capital of slate-pencil and marbles, and gradually
extending his operations until they aspired to the copper coinage of
this realm, in which he speculated to considerable advantage. Nor did
he trouble his borrowers with abstract calculations of figures, or
references to ready-reckoners; his simple rule of interest being all
comprised in the one golden sentence, ‘two-pence for every half-penny,’
which greatly simplified the accounts, and which, as a familiar precept,
more easily acquired and retained in the [[motifs/memory|memory]] than any known rule
of arithmetic, cannot be too strongly recommended to the notice of
capitalists, both large and small, and more especially of money-brokers
and bill-discounters. Indeed, to do these gentlemen justice, many of
them are to this day in the frequent habit of adopting it, with eminent
success.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 1

Presenta tutti gli altri


C'era una volta, in una parte appartata della contea del Devonshire, un certo signor Godfrey Nickleby: un gentiluomo degno di stima, che, avendo deciso piuttosto tardi nella vita che doveva sposarsi, e non essendo abbastanza giovane o abbastanza ricco da aspirare alla mano di una signora di nobile casato, aveva sposato una vecchia fiamma per puro affetto, che a sua volta lo aveva preso per la stessa ragione. Così due persone che non possono permettersi di giocare a carte per denaro, a volte si siedono a un tranquillo gioco per [[motifs/love|amore]].

Alcune persone di cattivo carattere che deridono la vita matrimoniale potrebbero forse suggerire, in questo punto, che la brava coppia sarebbe meglio paragonata a due protagonisti in un incontro di sparring, che, quando la fortuna è bassa e i sostenitori scarsi, si batteranno cavallerescamente, per il mero piacere della lotta; e in un certo senso questo paragone sarebbe valido; infatti, come la coppia avventurosa del [[settings/court|campo]] di Fives manderà poi in giro un cappello e si affiderà alla generosità degli spettatori per i mezzi per rallegrarsi, così il signor Godfrey Nickleby e la SUA partner, finita la luna di miele, guardano malinconicamente nel mondo, contando in non poca misura sulla fortuna per il miglioramento dei loro mezzi. Il reddito del signor Nickleby, al momento del suo [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]], oscillava tra sessanta e ottanta sterline ALL'ANNO.

Ci sono abbastanza persone nel mondo, Dio lo sa! e anche a [[settings/london|Londra]] (dove il signor Nickleby viveva in quei giorni) ma poche sono le lamentele per la scarsità della popolazione. È straordinario quanto a lungo un uomo possa guardare tra la folla senza scoprire il volto di un amico, ma è purtroppo vero. Il signor Nickleby guardò, e guardò, finché i suoi occhi divennero doloranti come il suo cuore, ma nessun amico apparve; e quando, stanco della ricerca, rivolse lo sguardo verso casa, vide ben poco lì per alleviare la sua stanchezza. Un pittore che ha fissato troppo a lungo un colore accecante, rinfresca la vista stordita guardando una tonalità più scura e cupa; ma tutto ciò che incontrava lo sguardo del signor Nickleby aveva un colore così nero e cupo, che sarebbe stato rinfrescato oltre ogni descrizione dal contrasto opposto.

Alla fine, dopo cinque anni, quando la signora Nickleby aveva dato al marito due figli maschi, e quel signore imbarazzato, convinto della necessità di provvedere alla sua famiglia, stava seriamente meditando una piccola speculazione commerciale assicurando la sua vita il prossimo trimestre e poi cadendo accidentalmente dalla cima del Monumento, una mattina arrivò, tramite la posta generale, una lettera bordata di nero per informarlo che suo zio, il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], era morto e gli aveva lasciato la maggior parte del suo modesto patrimonio, che ammontava in tutto a cinquemila sterline.

Poiché il defunto non aveva mai più fatto caso a suo nipote in vita sua, se non inviando al suo primogenito (che era stato battezzato con il suo nome, in un'impresa disperata) un cucchiaio d'argento in un astuccio di marocchino, che, dato che non aveva troppo da mangiare con esso, sembrava una specie di [[forms/satire|satira]] sul fatto che fosse nato senza quell'utile articolo di argenteria in bocca, il signor Godfrey Nickleby non poteva, all'inizio, credere alle notizie così trasmesse. Tuttavia, dopo un esame, si rivelarono essere rigorosamente corrette. Il vecchio gentiluomo, sembrava, aveva inteso lasciare tutto alla Royal Humane Society, e aveva infatti redatto un testamento a tal effetto; ma l'Istituzione, avendo avuto la sfortuna, alcuni mesi prima, di salvare la vita di un povero parente a cui pagava un'indennità settimanale di tre scellini e sei pence, aveva, in un accesso di esasperazione molto naturale, revocato la donazione in un codicillo, e lasciato tutto al signor Godfrey Nickleby; con una menzione speciale della sua indignazione, non solo contro la società per aver salvato la vita del povero parente, ma anche contro il povero parente stesso, per essersi lasciato salvare.

Con una parte di questa proprietà, il signor Godfrey Nickleby acquistò una piccola fattoria vicino a Dawlish nel Devonshire, dove si ritirò con la moglie e i due figli, per vivere degli interessi migliori che poteva ottenere per il resto del suo denaro e del poco che poteva produrre dalla sua terra. Le due cose prosperarono così [[motifs/well|bene]] insieme che, quando morì, circa quindici anni dopo questo periodo, e cinque anni dopo la moglie, fu in grado di lasciare al suo figlio maggiore, Ralph, tremila sterline in contanti, e al figlio minore, Nicholas, mille sterline e la fattoria, che era un possedimento terriero così piccolo come uno se ne potrebbe [[motifs/desire|desiderare]] di vedere.

Questi due fratelli erano stati educati insieme in una scuola a Exeter;
e, essendo abituati ad andare [[motifs/home|a casa]] una volta a settimana, avevano spesso sentito, dalle
labbra di loro madre, lunghi racconti delle sofferenze di loro padre nei
suoi giorni di [[concepts/poverty|povertà]], e dell'importanza del loro defunto zio nei suoi giorni
di agiatezza: racconti che producevano un'impressione molto diversa
nei due: mentre il più giovane, che era di indole timida e riservata,
non ne traeva altro che ammonimenti a evitare il grande mondo e ad
attaccarsi alla tranquilla routine della vita di campagna, Ralph, il
maggiore, deduceva dal racconto spesso ripetuto i due grandi
principi che la ricchezza è l'unica vera fonte di felicità e potere, e
che è lecito e giusto conseguirla con tutti i mezzi tranne il furto. ‘E,’
ragionava Ralph con se stesso, ‘se nessun bene è venuto dai soldi di mio
zio quando era vivo, un gran bene ne è venuto dopo che è morto, in quanto
mio padre li ha ora, e li sta mettendo da parte per me, il che è un
scopo altamente virtuoso; e, tornando al vecchio signore, il bene è
venuto anche a lui, perché ha avuto il piacere di pensarci tutta la
vita, e di essere invidiato e corteggiato da tutta la sua famiglia
oltre.’ E Ralph concludeva sempre questi soliloqui mentali arrivando
alla conclusione che non c'era niente di paragonabile al denaro.

Non limitandosi alla teoria, o permettendo alle sue facoltà di arrugginire,
anche a quell'età precoce, in mere speculazioni astratte, questo ragazzo
promettente iniziò a fare l'usuraio su piccola scala a scuola; investendo a buon
interesse un piccolo capitale di gessetti e biglie, e ampliando gradualmente
le sue operazioni fino a che non aspirarono alla monetazione di rame
di questo regno, in cui speculò con notevole vantaggio. E non si preoccupò
di disturbare i suoi debitori con calcoli astratti di cifre, o
con riferimenti a tabelle pronte; la sua semplice regola di interesse era
tutta compresa in un'unica frase d'oro, ‘due pence per ogni mezzo penny’,
che semplificava notevolmente i conti, e che, come precetto familiare,
più facilmente acquisito e conservato nella [[motifs/memory|memoria]] che qualsiasi nota regola
dell'aritmetica, non può essere raccomandato abbastanza fortemente all'attenzione
dei capitalisti, grandi e piccoli, e più specialmente dei banchieri
e degli scontisti di cambiali. Infatti, per fare giustizia a questi signori,
molti di loro sono ancora oggi abituati a adottarla, con eminente
successo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_02" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby — Chapter 1 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/hero,archetype/rebel,motif/death,motif/time,concept/doubt,concept/education,setting/london,character/nicholas_nickleby,character/nurse,character/ralph_nickleby"></span>


In like manner, did young [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] avoid all those minute and
intricate calculations of odd days, which nobody who has worked sums
in simple-interest can fail to have found most embarrassing, by
establishing the one general rule that all sums of principal and
interest should be paid on pocket-money day, that is to say, on
Saturday: and that whether a loan were contracted on the Monday, or on
the Friday, the amount of interest should be, in both cases, the same.
Indeed he argued, and with great show of reason, that it ought to be
rather more for one day than for five, inasmuch as the borrower might
in the former case be very fairly presumed to be in great extremity,
otherwise he would not borrow at all with such odds against him. This
fact is interesting, as illustrating the secret connection and sympathy
which always exist between great minds. Though Master [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] was
not at that [[motifs/time|time]] aware of it, the class of gentlemen before alluded to,
proceed on just the same principle in all their transactions.

From what we have said of this young gentleman, and the natural
admiration the reader will immediately conceive of his character, it may
perhaps be inferred that he is to be the [[archetypes/hero|hero]] of the work which we shall
presently begin. To set this point at rest, for once and for ever, we
hasten to undeceive them, and stride to its commencement.

On the [[motifs/death|death]] of his father, [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], who had been some [[motifs/time|time]]
before placed in a mercantile house in [[settings/london|London]], applied himself
passionately to his old pursuit of money-getting, in which he speedily
became so buried and absorbed, that he quite forgot his brother for many
years; and if, at times, a recollection of his old playfellow broke
upon him through the haze in which he lived--for gold conjures up a mist
about a man, more destructive of all his old senses and lulling to
his feelings than the fumes of charcoal--it brought along with it a
companion thought, that if they were intimate he would want to borrow
money of him. So, Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] shrugged his shoulders, and said
things were better as they were.

As for Nicholas, he lived a single man on the patrimonial estate until
he grew tired of living alone, and then he took to wife the daughter of
a neighbouring gentleman with a dower of one thousand pounds. This good
lady bore him two children, a son and a daughter, and when the son
was about nineteen, and the daughter fourteen, as near as we can
guess--impartial records of young ladies’ ages being, before the passing
of the new act, nowhere preserved in the registries of this country--Mr
Nickleby looked about him for the means of repairing his capital, now
sadly reduced by this increase in his family, and the expenses of their
[[concepts/education|education]].

‘Speculate with it,’ said Mrs. Nickleby.

‘Spec--u--late, my dear?’ said Mr. Nickleby, as though in [[concepts/doubt|doubt]].

‘Why not?’ asked Mrs. Nickleby.

‘Because, my dear, if we SHOULD lose it,’ rejoined Mr. Nickleby, who
was a slow and [[motifs/time|time]]-taking speaker, ‘if we SHOULD lose it, we shall no
longer be able to live, my dear.’

‘Fiddle,’ said Mrs. Nickleby.

‘I am not altogether sure of that, my dear,’ said Mr. Nickleby.

‘There’s Nicholas,’ pursued the lady, ‘quite a young man--it’s [[motifs/time|time]] he
was in the way of doing something for himself; and Kate too, poor girl,
without a penny in the world. Think of your brother! Would he be what he
is, if he hadn’t speculated?’

‘That’s true,’ replied Mr. Nickleby. ‘Very good, my dear. Yes. I WILL
speculate, my dear.’

Speculation is a round game; the players see little or nothing of their
cards at first starting; gains MAY be great--and so may losses. The run
of luck went against Mr. Nickleby. A mania prevailed, a bubble burst,
four stock-brokers took villa residences at Florence, four hundred
nobodies were ruined, and among them Mr. Nickleby.

‘The very house I live in,’ sighed the poor gentleman, ‘may be taken
from me tomorrow. Not an article of my old furniture, but will be sold
to strangers!’

The last reflection hurt him so much, that he took at once to his bed;
apparently resolved to keep that, at all events.

‘Cheer up, sir!’ said the apothecary.

‘You mustn’t let yourself be cast down, sir,’ said the [[characters/nurse|nurse]].

‘Such things happen every day,’ remarked the lawyer.

‘And it is very sinful to [[archetypes/rebel|rebel]] against them,’ whispered the clergyman.

‘And what no man with a family ought to do,’ added the neighbours.

Mr. Nickleby shook his head, and motioning them all out of the room,
embraced his wife and children, and having pressed them by turns to
his languidly beating heart, sunk exhausted on his pillow. They were
concerned to find that his reason went astray after this; for he
babbled, for a long [[motifs/time|time]], about the generosity and goodness of his
brother, and the merry old times when they were at school together.
This fit of wandering past, he solemnly commended them to One who never
deserted the widow or her fatherless children, and, smiling gently on
them, turned upon his face, and observed, that he thought he could fall
asleep.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Allo stesso modo, il giovane [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] evitava tutti quei minuti e
complicati calcoli di giorni dispari, che chiunque abbia fatto calcoli
di interessi semplici non può non aver trovato molto imbarazzanti, stabilendo
la regola generale che tutte le somme di capitale e interessi dovessero essere
pagate il giorno della paghetta, cioè il sabato: e che, sia che un prestito fosse
contratto il lunedì o il venerdì, l'ammontare degli interessi dovesse essere,
in entrambi i casi, lo stesso. Anzi, sosteneva, e con grande apparenza di ragione,
che dovrebbe essere piuttosto più alto per un giorno che per cinque, in quanto
il debitore potrebbe, nel primo caso, essere ragionevolmente presunto in grande estremo,
altrimenti non avrebbe preso a prestito affatto con tali svantaggi. Questo fatto è interessante,
in quanto illustra la segreta connessione e simpatia che esistono sempre tra grandi menti.
Sebbene il giovane [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] non fosse a quel [[motifs/time|tempo]] consapevole di ciò, la classe di gentiluomini
sopra accennata procede esattamente sullo stesso principio in tutte le loro transazioni.

Da quanto abbiamo detto di questo giovane gentiluomo, e dalla naturale
ammirazione che il lettore concepirà immediatamente per il suo carattere, si potrebbe
forse dedurre che egli sarà l'[[archetypes/hero|eroe]] dell'opera che stiamo
per iniziare. Per porre fine a questo dubbio, una volta per tutte, ci
affrettiamo a disingannarli e procediamo al suo inizio.

Alla [[motifs/death|morte]] del padre, [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], che era stato qualche [[motifs/time|tempo]] prima collocato in una casa commerciale a [[settings/london|Londra]], si dedicò con passione al suo vecchio obiettivo di guadagnare denaro, nel quale si immerse e si assorbì così rapidamente, che dimenticò completamente suo fratello per molti anni; e se, a volte, un ricordo del suo vecchio compagno di giochi gli si presentava attraverso la nebbia in cui viveva - perché l'oro evoca una foschia intorno a un uomo, più distruttiva di tutti i suoi vecchi sensi e più addormentante per i suoi sentimenti dei fumi del carbone - questo ricordo portava con sé un pensiero compagno, che se fossero stati intimi lui avrebbe voluto chiedergli in prestito del denaro. Così, il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] si strinse nelle spalle e disse che le cose andavano meglio così come erano.

Per quanto riguarda Nicholas, visse da scapolo nella proprietà patrimoniale fino a quando si stancò di vivere solo, e allora sposò la figlia di un gentiluomo del vicinato con una dote di mille sterline. Questa brava donna gli diede due figli, un maschio e una femmina, e quando il figlio aveva circa diciannove anni e la figlia quattordici, per quanto possiamo indovinare - dato che i registri imparziali delle età delle giovani signore, prima dell'approvazione del nuovo atto, non erano conservati da nessuna parte nei registri di questo paese - il signor Nickleby si guardò intorno in cerca di mezzi per riparare il suo capitale, ormai tristemente ridotto da questo aumento della sua famiglia e dalle spese della loro [[concepts/education|educazione]].

«Speculare con esso», disse la signora Nickleby.

«Spec--u--lare, mia cara?» disse il signor Nickleby, come se fosse in [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]].

«Perché no?» chiese la signora Nickleby.

«Perché, mia cara, se DOVESSIMO perderla», replicò il signor Nickleby, che era un uomo lento e di [[motifs/time|parole]] ponderate, «se DOVESSIMO perderla, non saremmo più in grado di vivere, mia cara.»

«Violino», disse la signora Nickleby.

«Non ne sono del tutto sicuro, mia cara», disse il signor Nickleby.

«C'è Nicholas», continuò la signora, «un giovane uomo, è [[motifs/time|ora]] che
si mettesse a fare qualcosa per conto suo; e anche Kate, povera ragazza,
senza un soldo al mondo. Pensate a vostro fratello! Sarebbe quello che è
se non avesse speculato?»

‘È vero’, rispose il signor Nickleby. ‘Molto bene, mia cara. Sì. Speculerò, mia cara.’

La speculazione è un gioco a tutto tondo; all'inizio i giocatori vedono poco o nulla delle loro carte; i guadagni possono essere grandi, e così possono esserlo le perdite. La fortuna si è rivoltata contro il signor Nickleby. Si diffuse una mania, scoppiò una bolla, quattro agenti di borsa si comprarono ville a Firenze, quattrocento nullità andarono in rovina, e tra questi il signor Nickleby.

«La stessa casa in cui vivo», sospirò il povero signore, «potrebbe essere
tolta a me domani. Non un articolo del mio vecchio mobilio, ma sarà venduto
agli estranei!»

L'ultima riflessione lo ferì così tanto che si mise subito a letto;
e sembrava deciso a restarci, a ogni costo.

«Consolatevi, signore!» disse il farmacista.

«Non dovete lasciarvi abbattere, signore», disse la [[characters/nurse|balia]].

«Queste cose succedono tutti i giorni», osservò l'avvocato.

«E' un peccato gravissimo [[archetypes/rebel|ribellarsi]] contro di loro», sussurrò il prete.

«E ciò che nessun uomo con una famiglia dovrebbe fare», aggiunsero i vicini.

Il signor Nickleby scosse la testa e, facendo cenno a tutti di uscire dalla stanza, abbracciò la moglie e i figli, e dopo averli a turno stretti al suo cuore che batteva languidamente, cadde esausto sul cuscino. Erano preoccupati nel constatare che dopo ciò la sua ragione si smarriva; infatti, per un lungo [[motifs/time|periodo]], borbottava della generosità e della bontà di suo fratello, e dei vecchi tempi felici quando erano insieme a scuola. Passata questa crisi di delirio, raccomandò loro solennemente Colui che non abbandona mai la vedova o i suoi figli orfani, e, sorridendo dolcemente a loro, si voltò sulla faccia, e osservò che pensava di poter addormentarsi.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_02--part_01" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby — Chapter 2 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 02" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/autumn,motif/leaves,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,motif/wind,motif/window,concept/melancholy,form/fragment,setting/london,character/nicholas_nickleby,character/ralph_nickleby"></span>


CHAPTER 2

Of Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], and his Establishments, and his Undertakings, and
of a great Joint Stock Company of vast national Importance


Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] was not, strictly speaking, what you would call
a merchant, neither was he a banker, nor an attorney, nor a special
pleader, nor a notary. He was certainly not a tradesman, and still less
could he lay any claim to the title of a professional gentleman; for it
would have been impossible to mention any recognised profession to which
he belonged. Nevertheless, as he lived in a spacious house in Golden
Square, which, in addition to a brass plate upon the street-door, had
another brass plate two sizes and a half smaller upon the left hand
door-post, surrounding a brass model of an infant’s fist grasping a
[[forms/fragment|fragment]] of a skewer, and displaying the word ‘Office,’ it was clear
that Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] did, or pretended to do, business of some kind;
and the fact, if it required any further circumstantial evidence, was
abundantly demonstrated by the diurnal attendance, between the hours of
half-past nine and five, of a sallow-faced man in rusty brown, who sat
upon an uncommonly hard stool in a species of butler’s pantry at the end
of the passage, and always had a pen behind his ear when he answered the
bell.

Although a few members of the graver professions live about Golden
Square, it is not exactly in anybody’s way to or from anywhere. It is
one of the squares that have been; a quarter of the town that has gone
down in the world, and taken to letting lodgings. Many of its first
and second floors are let, furnished, to single gentlemen; and it
takes boarders besides. It is a great resort of foreigners. The
dark-complexioned men who wear large rings, and heavy watch-guards, and
bushy whiskers, and who congregate under the Opera Colonnade, and about
the box-office in the season, between four and five in the afternoon,
when they give away the orders,--all live in Golden Square, or within a
street of it. Two or three violins and a [[motifs/wind|wind]] instrument from the Opera
band reside within its precincts. Its boarding-houses are musical, and
the notes of pianos and harps float in the evening [[motifs/time|time]] round the head
of the mournful statue, the guardian genius of a little wilderness of
shrubs, in the centre of the square. On a [[motifs/summer|summer]]’s [[motifs/night|night]], windows
are thrown open, and groups of swarthy moustached men are seen by the
passer-by, lounging at the casements, and smoking fearfully. Sounds of
gruff voices practising vocal music invade the evening’s [[motifs/silence|silence]]; and
the fumes of choice tobacco scent the air. There, snuff and cigars,
and German pipes and flutes, and violins and violoncellos, divide the
supremacy between them. It is the region of song and smoke. Street bands
are on their mettle in Golden Square; and itinerant glee-singers quaver
involuntarily as they raise their voices within its boundaries.

This would not seem a spot very [[motifs/well|well]] adapted to the transaction of
business; but Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] had lived there, notwithstanding, for
many years, and uttered no complaint on that score. He knew nobody round
about, and nobody knew him, although he enjoyed the reputation of being
immensely rich. The tradesmen held that he was a sort of lawyer, and
the other neighbours opined that he was a kind of general agent; both
of which guesses were as correct and definite as guesses about other
people’s affairs usually are, or need to be.

Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] sat in his private office one morning, ready dressed
to walk abroad. He wore a bottle-green spencer over a blue coat; a white
waistcoat, grey mixture pantaloons, and Wellington boots drawn over
them. The corner of a small-plaited shirt-frill struggled out, as if
insisting to show itself, from between his chin and the top button of
his spencer; and the latter garment was not made low enough to conceal
a long gold watch-chain, composed of a series of plain rings, which had
its beginning at the handle of a gold repeater in Mr. Nickleby’s pocket,
and its termination in two little keys: one belonging to the watch
itself, and the other to some patent padlock. He wore a sprinkling of
powder upon his head, as if to make himself look benevolent; but if
that were his purpose, he would perhaps have done better to powder his
countenance also, for there was something in its very wrinkles, and
in his cold restless eye, which seemed to tell of cunning that would
announce itself in spite of him. However this might be, there he was;
and as he was all alone, neither the powder, nor the wrinkles, nor the
eyes, had the smallest effect, good or bad, upon anybody just then, and
are consequently no business of ours just now.

Mr. Nickleby closed an account-book which lay on his desk, and, throwing
himself back in his chair, gazed with an air of abstraction through the
dirty [[motifs/window|window]]. Some [[settings/london|London]] houses have a [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] little plot of ground
behind them, usually fenced in by four high whitewashed walls, and
frowned upon by stacks of chimneys: in which there withers on, from
year to year, a crippled tree, that makes a show of putting forth a few
[[motifs/leaves|leaves]] late in [[motifs/autumn|autumn]] when other trees shed theirs, and, drooping in
the effort, lingers on, all crackled and smoke-dried, till the following
season, when it repeats the same process, and perhaps, if the weather
be particularly genial, even tempts some rheumatic sparrow to chirrup
in its branches. People sometimes call these dark yards ‘gardens’; it
is not supposed that they were ever planted, but rather that they are
pieces of unreclaimed land, with the withered vegetation of the original
brick-field. No man thinks of walking in this desolate place, or of
turning it to any account. A few hampers, half-a-dozen broken bottles,
and such-like rubbish, may be thrown there, when the tenant first moves
in, but nothing more; and there they remain until he goes away again:
the damp straw taking just as long to moulder as it thinks proper:
and mingling with the scanty box, and stunted everbrowns, and broken
flower-pots, that are scattered mournfully about--a prey to ‘blacks’ and
dirt.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 2

Di [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Mr. Ralph Nickleby]], e dei suoi Stabilimenti, e delle sue Imprese, e
di una grande Società in accomandita di enorme importanza nazionale


Il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] non era, a dir la verità, quel che si potrebbe chiamare un commerciante, né era un banchiere, né un avvocato, né un procuratore, né un notaio. Non era certamente un artigiano, e ancor meno poteva rivendicare il titolo di gentiluomo professionista; poiché sarebbe stato impossibile menzionare una professione riconosciuta a cui appartenesse. Tuttavia, poiché viveva in una spaziosa casa in Golden Square, che, oltre a una targa di ottone sulla porta d'ingresso, aveva un'altra targa di ottone due misure e mezzo più piccola sul montante sinistro della porta, che circondava un modello di ottone di un pugno infantile che stringeva un [[forms/fragment|frammento]] di uno stuzzicadenti, e che mostrava la parola "Ufficio", era chiaro che il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] faceva, o fingeva di fare, affari di qualche tipo; e il fatto, se avesse richiesto ulteriori prove circostanziali, era ampiamente dimostrato dalla presenza quotidiana, tra le ore di mezz'ora dopo le nove e le cinque, di un uomo dal viso giallastro in un abito marrone scolorito, che sedeva su uno sgabello particolarmente duro in una specie di dispensa da maggiordomo alla fine del corridoio, e che aveva sempre una penna dietro l'orecchio quando rispondeva al campanello.

Sebbene alcuni membri delle professioni più serie vivano intorno a Golden Square, non è esattamente sulla strada di qualcuno da o verso nessun posto. È una delle piazze che sono state; un quartiere della città che è decaduto e si è messo a affittare camere. Molti dei suoi piani terra e primi piani sono affittati, ammobiliati, a signori single; e inoltre accoglie pensionanti. È un grande ritrovo di stranieri. Gli uomini dal complesso scuro che indossano grandi anelli, pesanti catene per l'orologio e baffi folti, e che si radunano sotto la Colonnata dell'Opera e intorno alla biglietteria in stagione, tra le quattro e le cinque del pomeriggio, quando distribuiscono gli inviti,--tutti vivono a Golden Square, o a una strada di distanza. Due o tre violini e uno strumento a [[motifs/wind|fiato]] della banda dell'Opera risiedono nei suoi confini. Le sue pensioni sono musicali, e le note di pianoforti e arpe fluttuano nella sera intorno alla testa della statua malinconica, il genio tutelare di un piccolo deserto di cespugli, al centro della piazza. In una [[motifs/summer|serata]] d'[[motifs/night|estate]], le finestre sono spalancate, e il passante vede gruppi di uomini scuri con baffi che si affacciano alle finestre, fumando in modo spaventoso. I suoni di voci roche che esercitano la musica vocale invadono il [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] serale; e i fumi del tabacco pregiato profumano l'aria. Lì, tabacco da fiuto e sigari, pipe tedesche e flauti, violini e violoncelli, si dividono la supremazia. È la regione della canzone e del fumo. Le bande di strada sono al massimo della loro forma a Golden Square; e i cantanti itineranti tremolano involontariamente quando alzano la voce nei suoi confini.

Questo non sembrerebbe un luogo molto [[motifs/well|adatto]] agli affari; ma il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] vi aveva vissuto per molti anni, senza mai lamentarsi. Non conosceva nessuno in giro, e nessuno conosceva lui, sebbene godesse della reputazione di essere immensamente ricco. I commercianti sostenevano che fosse una specie di avvocato, e gli altri vicini erano dell'opinione che fosse una specie di agente generale; entrambe le ipotesi erano altrettanto corrette e precise quanto lo sono, e devono essere, le ipotesi sugli affari altrui.

Il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] sedeva nel suo ufficio privato una mattina, pronto vestito per uscire. Indossava uno spencer verde bottiglia sopra un soprabito blu; un panciotto bianco, pantaloni grigi a mescola e stivali Wellington calzati sopra. L'angolo di un piccolo frill della camicia si affacciava, come se insistesse per mostrarsi, tra il suo mento e il primo bottone dello spencer; e quest'ultimo indumento non era abbastanza lungo da nascondere una lunga catena d'oro, composta da una serie di anelli semplici, che aveva inizio dal manico di un orologio ripetitore d'oro nella tasca del signor Nickleby, e la sua terminazione in due piccole chiavi: una appartenente all'orologio stesso, e l'altra a qualche lucchetto brevettato. Portava una spolverata di polvere sui capelli, come se volesse farsi apparire benevolo; ma se questo era il suo scopo, forse avrebbe fatto meglio a polverizzare anche il suo volto, perché c'era qualcosa nelle sue stesse rughe, e nel suo freddo occhio inquieto, che sembrava raccontare di una furberia che si sarebbe manifestata nonostante lui. Comunque fosse, eccolo lì; e poiché era tutto solo, né la polvere, né le rughe, né gli occhi, avevano il minimo effetto, buono o cattivo, su qualcuno in quel momento, e di conseguenza non sono affari nostri proprio ora.

Mr. Nickleby chiuse un libro mastro che giaceva sulla sua scrivania e, appoggiandosi allo schienale della sedia, fissò con aria assorta attraverso la sporca [[motifs/window|finestra]]. Alcune case di [[settings/london|Londra]] hanno un piccolo appezzamento di terreno [[concepts/melancholy|malinconico]] dietro di loro, solitamente recintato da quattro alte mura imbiancate a calce, e sovrastato da cumuli di ciminiere: in cui un albero storpio appassisce anno dopo anno, facendo mostra di mettere fuori qualche [[motifs/leaves|foglia]] tardi in [[motifs/autumn|autunno]] quando gli altri alberi ne perdono le loro, e, curvandosi nello sforzo, rimane lì, tutto raggrinzito e secco dal fumo, fino alla stagione successiva, quando ripete lo stesso processo, e forse, se il tempo è particolarmente mite, riesce persino a indurre qualche sparviero reumatico a cinguettare tra i suoi rami. A volte la gente chiama questi cortili bui "giardini"; non si pensa che siano mai stati piantati, ma piuttosto che siano pezzi di terra non bonificata, con la vegetazione appassita del campo di mattoni originale. Nessuno pensa di passeggiare in questo luogo desolato, o di utilizzarlo in alcun modo. Alcuni cesti, mezza dozzina di bottiglie rotte e simili rifiuti possono essere gettati lì quando ilinquilino si trasferisce, ma niente di più; e lì rimangono fino a quando non se ne va: la paglia umida impiega esattamente il tempo che ritiene opportuno per decomporre: e si mescola con il rado bosso, gli stentati sempreverdi e i vasi di fiori rotti, che sono sparsi tristemente intorno - preda di "macchie" e sporcizia.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_02--part_02" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby — Chapter 2 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 02" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/fool,motif/city,motif/clock,motif/cross,motif/home,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/window,concept/charity,setting/london,character/nicholas_nickleby,character/ralph_nickleby"></span>


It was into a place of this kind that Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] gazed, as he sat
with his hands in his pockets looking out of the [[motifs/window|window]]. He had fixed
his eyes upon a distorted fir tree, planted by some former tenant in a
tub that had once been green, and left there, years before, to rot
away piecemeal. There was nothing very inviting in the object, but Mr
Nickleby was wrapt in a brown study, and sat contemplating it with far
greater attention than, in a more conscious mood, he would have deigned
to bestow upon the rarest exotic. At length, his eyes wandered to a
little dirty [[motifs/window|window]] on the left, through which the face of the clerk
was dimly visible; that worthy chancing to look up, he beckoned him to
attend.

In obedience to this summons the clerk got off the high stool (to which
he had communicated a high polish by countless gettings off and on),
and presented himself in Mr. Nickleby’s room. He was a tall man of middle
age, with two goggle eyes whereof one was a fixture, a rubicund nose,
a cadaverous face, and a suit of clothes (if the term be allowable
when they suited him not at all) much the worse for wear, very much too
small, and placed upon such a short allowance of buttons that it was
marvellous how he contrived to keep them on.

‘Was that half-past twelve, Noggs?’ said Mr. Nickleby, in a sharp and
grating voice.

‘Not more than five-and-twenty minutes by the--’ Noggs was going to
add public-house [[motifs/clock|clock]], but recollecting himself, substituted ‘regular
[[motifs/time|time]].’

‘My watch has stopped,’ said Mr. Nickleby; ‘I don’t know from what
cause.’

‘Not wound up,’ said Noggs.

‘Yes it is,’ said Mr. Nickleby.

‘Over-wound then,’ rejoined Noggs.

‘That can’t very [[motifs/well|well]] be,’ observed Mr. Nickleby.

‘Must be,’ said Noggs.

‘[[motifs/well|Well]]!’ said Mr. Nickleby, putting the repeater back in his pocket;
‘perhaps it is.’

Noggs gave a peculiar grunt, as was his custom at the end of all
disputes with his master, to imply that he (Noggs) triumphed; and (as he
rarely spoke to anybody unless somebody spoke to him) fell into a grim
[[motifs/silence|silence]], and rubbed his hands slowly over each other: cracking the
joints of his fingers, and squeezing them into all possible distortions.
The incessant performance of this routine on every occasion, and the
communication of a fixed and rigid look to his unaffected eye, so as to
make it uniform with the other, and to render it impossible for anybody
to determine where or at what he was looking, were two among the
numerous peculiarities of Mr. Noggs, which struck an inexperienced
observer at first sight.

‘I am going to the [[settings/london|London]] Tavern this morning,’ said Mr. Nickleby.

‘Public meeting?’ inquired Noggs.

Mr. Nickleby nodded. ‘I expect a letter from the solicitor respecting
that mortgage of Ruddle’s. If it comes at all, it will be here by the
two o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] delivery. I shall leave the [[motifs/city|city]] about that [[motifs/time|time]] and walk
to Charing [[motifs/cross|Cross]] on the left-hand side of the way; if there are any
letters, come and meet me, and bring them with you.’

Noggs nodded; and as he nodded, there came a ring at the office bell.
The master looked up from his papers, and the clerk calmly remained in a
stationary position.

‘The bell,’ said Noggs, as though in explanation. ‘At [[motifs/home|home]]?’

‘Yes.’

‘To anybody?’

‘Yes.’

‘To the tax-gatherer?’

‘No! Let him call again.’

Noggs gave vent to his usual grunt, as much as to say ‘I thought so!’
and, the ring being repeated, went to the door, whence he presently
returned, ushering in, by the name of Mr. Bonney, a pale gentleman in a
violent hurry, who, with his hair standing up in great disorder all over
his head, and a very narrow white cravat tied loosely round his throat,
looked as if he had been knocked up in the [[motifs/night|night]] and had not dressed
himself since.

‘My dear Nickleby,’ said the gentleman, taking off a white hat which was
so full of papers that it would scarcely stick upon his head, ‘there’s
not a moment to lose; I have a cab at the door. Sir Matthew Pupker takes
the chair, and three members of Parliament are positively coming. I have
seen two of them safely out of bed. The third, who was at Crockford’s
all [[motifs/night|night]], has just gone [[motifs/home|home]] to put a clean shirt on, and take a bottle
or two of soda [[motifs/water|water]], and will certainly be with us, in [[motifs/time|time]] to address
the meeting. He is a little excited by last [[motifs/night|night]], but never mind that;
he always speaks the stronger for it.’

‘It seems to promise pretty [[motifs/well|well]],’ said Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], whose
deliberate manner was strongly opposed to the vivacity of the other man
of business.

‘Pretty [[motifs/well|well]]!’ echoed Mr. Bonney. ‘It’s the finest idea that was ever
started. “United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking
and Punctual Delivery Company. Capital, five millions, in five hundred
thousand shares of ten pounds each.” Why the very name will get the
shares up to a premium in ten days.’

‘And when they ARE at a premium,’ said Mr. [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], smiling.

‘When they are, you know what to do with them as [[motifs/well|well]] as any man alive,
and how to back quietly out at the right [[motifs/time|time]],’ said Mr. Bonney, slapping
the capitalist familiarly on the shoulder. ‘By-the-bye, what a VERY
remarkable man that clerk of yours is.’

‘Yes, poor devil!’ replied Ralph, drawing on his gloves. ‘Though Newman
Noggs kept his horses and hounds once.’

‘Ay, ay?’ said the other carelessly.

‘Yes,’ continued Ralph, ‘and not many years ago either; but he
squandered his money, invested it anyhow, borrowed at interest, and in
short made first a thorough [[archetypes/fool|fool]] of himself, and then a beggar. He took
to drinking, and had a touch of paralysis, and then came here to borrow
a pound, as in his better days I had--’

‘Done business with him,’ said Mr. Bonney with a meaning look.

‘Just so,’ replied Ralph; ‘I couldn’t lend it, you know.’

‘Oh, of course not.’

‘But as I wanted a clerk just then, to open the door and so forth, I
took him out of [[concepts/charity|charity]], and he has remained with me ever since. He is
a little mad, I think,’ said Mr. Nickleby, calling up a charitable look,
‘but he is useful enough, poor creature--useful enough.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Fu in un luogo di questo genere che il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]] si soffermò a guardare, mentre sedeva
con le mani in tasca e lo sguardo rivolto fuori dalla [[motifs/window|finestra]]. Aveva fissato
gli occhi su un abete deformato, piantato da qualche precedente inquilino in un
vaso che un tempo era stato verde, e lasciato lì, anni prima, a marcire
a poco a poco. Non c'era nulla di particolarmente invitante nell'oggetto, ma il
signor Nickleby era immerso in profonde riflessioni e lo contemplava con un'attenzione
molto maggiore di quella che, in uno stato d'animo più consapevole, avrebbe degnato
di concedere al più raro esotico. Alla fine, i suoi occhi si spostarono su una
piccola e sporca [[motifs/window|finestra]] sulla sinistra, attraverso la quale il volto del commesso
era appena visibile; poiché quest'ultimo alzò lo sguardo, il signor Nickleby lo invitò ad avvicinarsi.

In obbedienza a questo invito, il commesso scese dallo sgabello alto (che aveva reso lucido grazie a innumerevoli salite e discese) e si presentò nella stanza del signor Nickleby. Era un uomo alto di mezza età, con due occhi sporgenti, di cui uno fisso, un naso rubizzo, un volto cadaverico e un abito (se il termine è consentito quando non gli calzava affatto) molto malandato, troppo piccolo e con una quantità di bottoni così scarsa che era un miracolo come riuscisse a tenerli attaccati.

«Erano le dodici e mezza, Noggs?» disse il signor Nickleby con voce aspra e stridente.

«Non più di venticinque minuti secondo il--» Noggs stava per aggiungere orologio del [[motifs/clock|pubblico]] [[motifs/time|locale]], ma ricordandosi, sostituì con «orario [[motifs/time|regolare]].»

‘Il mio orologio si è fermato’, disse il signor Nickleby, ‘non so per quale motivo’.

«Non è stato avvolto», disse Noggs.

«Sì, è così», disse il signor Nickleby.

«Eccessivamente carica, allora», ribatté Noggs.

«Non può essere [[motifs/well|così]]», osservò il signor Nickleby.

«Deve essere», disse Noggs.

«[[motifs/well|Beh]]!» disse il signor Nickleby, rimettendo il ripetitore in tasca; «forse lo è.»

Noggs emise un grugnito particolare, come era sua abitudine alla fine di tutte le dispute con il suo padrone, per implicare che lui (Noggs) trionfava; e (poiché raramente parlava a qualcuno a meno che qualcuno non parlasse a lui) cadde in un cupo [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] e si strofinò lentamente le mani l'una contro l'altra: schioccando le articolazioni delle dita e torcendole in tutte le possibili distorsioni. L'incessante esecuzione di questa routine in ogni occasione e la comunicazione di uno sguardo fisso e rigido al suo occhio non affetto, in modo da renderlo uniforme con l'altro e rendere impossibile per chiunque determinare dove o su cosa stesse guardando, erano due tra le numerose peculiarità del signor Noggs, che colpivano un osservatore inesperto a prima vista.

«Stamattina vado alla [[settings/london|London]] Tavern», disse il signor Nickleby.

«Riunione pubblica?» chiese Noggs.

Il signor Nickleby annuì. «Aspetto una lettera dall'avvocato riguardo
a quel mutuo di Ruddle. Se arriva, sarà qui entro la consegna delle
due in [[motifs/clock|punto]]. Lascerò la [[motifs/city|città]] circa a quell'[[motifs/time|ora]] e camminerò
fino a Charing [[motifs/cross|Cross]] sul lato sinistro della strada; se ci sono lettere, vieni a incontrarmi e portale con te.»

Noggs annuì; e mentre annuiva, squillò il campanello dell'ufficio.
Il padrone alzò gli occhi dai suoi documenti, e il commesso rimase tranquillamente immobile.

«La [[motifs/home|campana]]», disse Noggs, come per spiegare. «A [[motifs/home|casa]]?»

'Sì, davvero.'

‘A chiunque?’

'Sì, davvero.'

'Al riscossore delle tasse?'

'No! Che chiami di nuovo.'

Noggs diede sfogo al suo solito grugnito, come per dire «Lo sapevo!»
e, dato che il campanello suonava di nuovo, andò alla porta, da cui tornò poco dopo
facendo entrare, col nome di signor Bonney, un gentiluomo pallido in grande fretta, che, con i capelli che gli stavano dritti in grande disordine su tutta la testa, e una cravatta bianca molto stretta legata con noncuranza intorno al collo, sembrava che fosse stato svegliato nel [[motifs/night|mezzo]] della notte e non si fosse vestito da allora.

«Mio caro Nickleby», disse il gentiluomo, togliendosi un cappello bianco così pieno di carte che a malapena gli stava in testa, «non c'è un momento da perdere; ho una carrozza alla porta. Sir Matthew Pupker presiede, e tre membri del Parlamento stanno sicuramente arrivando. Ne ho visti due al sicuro fuori dal letto. Il terzo, che era a Crockford tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]], è appena andato [[motifs/home|a casa]] per mettersi una camicia pulita e prendere una bottiglia o due di [[motifs/water|acqua]] gassata, e sarà certamente con noi, in [[motifs/time|tempo]] per indirizzare l'assemblea. È un po' eccitato per l'ultima [[motifs/night|notte]], ma non importa; parla sempre più forte per questo».

«Sembra promettere abbastanza [[motifs/well|bene]]», disse il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], il cui
modo di fare ponderato era in forte contrasto con la vivacità dell'altro
uomo d'affari.

«Abbastanza [[motifs/well|bene]]!» fece eco il signor Bonney. «È l'idea più brillante che sia mai stata concepita. "United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking and Punctual Delivery Company. Capitale, cinque milioni, in cinquecentomila azioni da dieci sterline ciascuna." Per il semplice nome le azioni saliranno a un premio in dieci giorni.»

«E quando sono davvero preziosi», disse il signor [[characters/ralph-nickleby|Ralph Nickleby]], sorridendo.

«Quando lo sono, sapete cosa fare con loro altrettanto [[motifs/well|bene]] di qualsiasi altro uomo in vita,
e come ritirarvi silenziosamente al momento giusto»,» disse il signor Bonney, dando
familiaremente una pacca sulla spalla al capitalista. «A proposito, che uomo
VERAMENTE straordinario è quel vostro impiegato.»

«Sì, povero diavolo!» rispose Ralph, infilando i guanti. «Anche se Newman Noggs aveva cavalli e cani una volta.»

«Ah, ah?» disse l'altro con noncuranza.

«Sì», continuò Ralph, «e non molti anni fa; ma lui
ha sperperato i suoi soldi, li ha investiti alla cieca, ha preso a interesse, e
in breve prima ha fatto un completo [[archetypes/fool|sciocco]] di se stesso, e poi un mendicante. Si è messo a bere, ha avuto un attacco di paralisi, e poi è venuto qui a chiedere in prestito una sterlina, come ai vecchi tempi avevo io--»

«Ho fatto affari con lui», disse il signor Bonney con uno sguardo significativo.

'Esattamente', rispose Ralph; 'non potevo prestarglielo, lo sai.'

'Oh, naturalmente no.'

«Ma poiché in quel momento avevo bisogno di un impiegato per aprire la porta e cose del genere, lo presi per [[concepts/charity|carità]] e da allora è rimasto con me. È un po' pazzo, credo», disse il signor Nickleby, assumendo un'espressione benevola, «ma è abbastanza utile, poveretto, abbastanza utile.»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_02--part_03" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby — Chapter 2 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 02" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="topos/double,motif/clock,motif/desire,motif/road,motif/time,concept/hope,character/newman_noggs,character/nicholas_nickleby"></span>


The kind-hearted gentleman omitted to add that [[characters/newman-noggs|Newman Noggs]], being
utterly destitute, served him for rather less than the usual wages of a
boy of thirteen; and likewise failed to mention in his hasty chronicle,
that his eccentric taciturnity rendered him an especially valuable
person in a place where much business was done, of which it was
desirable no mention should be made out of doors. The other gentleman
was plainly impatient to be gone, however, and as they hurried into the
hackney cabriolet immediately afterwards, perhaps Mr. Nickleby forgot to
mention circumstances so unimportant.

There was a great bustle in Bishopsgate Street Within, as they drew up,
and (it being a windy day) half-a-dozen men were tacking across the [[motifs/road|road]]
under a press of paper, bearing gigantic announcements that a Public
Meeting would be holden at one o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] precisely, to take into
consideration the propriety of petitioning Parliament in favour of the
United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking and Punctual
Delivery Company, capital five millions, in five hundred thousand shares
of ten pounds each; which sums were duly set forth in fat black figures
of considerable size. Mr. Bonney elbowed his way briskly upstairs,
receiving in his progress many low bows from the waiters who stood on
the landings to show the way; and, followed by Mr. Nickleby, dived into a
suite of apartments behind the great public room: in the second of which
was a business-looking table, and several business-looking people.

‘Hear!’ cried a gentleman with a [[topoi/double|double]] chin, as Mr. Bonney presented
himself. ‘Chair, gentlemen, chair!’

The new-comers were received with universal approbation, and Mr. Bonney
bustled up to the top of the table, took off his hat, ran his fingers
through his hair, and knocked a hackney-coachman’s knock on the table
with a little hammer: whereat several gentlemen cried ‘Hear!’ and nodded
slightly to each other, as much as to say what spirited conduct that
was. Just at this moment, a waiter, feverish with agitation, tore into
the room, and throwing the door open with a crash, shouted ‘Sir Matthew
Pupker!’

The committee stood up and clapped their hands for joy, and while they
were clapping them, in came Sir Matthew Pupker, attended by two live
members of Parliament, one Irish and one Scotch, all smiling and bowing,
and looking so pleasant that it seemed a perfect marvel how any
man could have the heart to vote against them. Sir Matthew Pupker
especially, who had a little round head with a flaxen wig on the top
of it, fell into such a paroxysm of bows, that the wig threatened to
be jerked off, every instant. When these symptoms had in some degree
subsided, the gentlemen who were on speaking terms with Sir Matthew
Pupker, or the two other members, crowded round them in three little
groups, near one or other of which the gentlemen who were NOT on
speaking terms with Sir Matthew Pupker or the two other members, stood
lingering, and smiling, and rubbing their hands, in the desperate [[concepts/hope|hope]]
of something turning up which might bring them into notice. All this
[[motifs/time|time]], Sir Matthew Pupker and the two other members were relating to
their separate circles what the intentions of government were, about
taking up the bill; with a full account of what the government had said
in a whisper the last [[motifs/time|time]] they dined with it, and how the government
had been observed to wink when it said so; from which premises they were
at no loss to draw the conclusion, that if the government had one
object more at heart than another, that one object was the welfare and
advantage of the United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet
Baking and Punctual Delivery Company.

Meanwhile, and pending the arrangement of the proceedings, and a fair
division of the speechifying, the public in the large room were eyeing,
by turns, the empty platform, and the ladies in the Music Gallery. In
these amusements the greater portion of them had been occupied for a
couple of hours before, and as the most agreeable diversions pall upon
the taste on a too protracted enjoyment of them, the sterner spirits now
began to hammer the floor with their boot-heels, and to express their
dissatisfaction by various hoots and cries. These vocal exertions,
emanating from the people who had been there longest, naturally
proceeded from those who were nearest to the platform and furthest from
the policemen in attendance, who having no great mind to fight their way
through the crowd, but entertaining nevertheless a praiseworthy [[motifs/desire|desire]]
to do something to quell the disturbance, immediately began to drag
forth, by the coat tails and collars, all the quiet people near the
door; at the same [[motifs/time|time]] dealing out various smart and tingling blows with
their truncheons, after the manner of that ingenious actor, Mr. Punch:
whose brilliant example, both in the fashion of his weapons and their
use, this branch of the executive occasionally follows.

Several very exciting skirmishes were in progress, when a loud shout
attracted the attention even of the belligerents, and then there poured
on to the platform, from a door at the side, a long line of gentlemen
with their hats off, all looking behind them, and uttering vociferous
cheers; the cause whereof was sufficiently explained when Sir Matthew
Pupker and the two other real members of Parliament came to the front,
amidst deafening shouts, and testified to each other in dumb motions
that they had never seen such a glorious sight as that, in the whole
course of their public career.

At length, and at last, the assembly left off shouting, but Sir Matthew
Pupker being voted into the chair, they underwent a relapse which lasted
five minutes. This over, Sir Matthew Pupker went on to say what must be
his feelings on that great occasion, and what must be that occasion
in the eyes of the world, and what must be the intelligence of
his fellow-countrymen before him, and what must be the wealth and
respectability of his honourable friends behind him, and lastly, what
must be the importance to the wealth, the happiness, the comfort, the
liberty, the very existence of a free and great people, of such an
Institution as the United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet
Baking and Punctual Delivery Company!


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Il gentiluomo di buon cuore dimenticò di aggiungere che [[characters/newman-noggs|Newman Noggs]], essendo
completamente indigente, lavorava per lui per uno stipendio piuttosto inferiore a quello
abituale di un ragazzo di tredici anni; e allo stesso modo non menzionò nella sua affrettata cronaca
che la sua eccentrica taciturnità lo rendeva una persona particolarmente preziosa
in un luogo dove si svolgevano molte attività, delle quali era
desiderabile che non se ne facesse menzione fuori. L'altro gentiluomo
era chiaramente impaziente di andarsene, tuttavia, e poiché si affrettarono a salire sul cabriolet pubblico subito dopo, forse il signor Nickleby dimenticò di
menzionare circostanze così insignificanti.

C'era grande trambusto a Bishopsgate Street Within, mentre si avvicinavano, e (essendo una giornata ventosa) mezza dozzina di uomini stavano attraversando la [[motifs/road|strada]] con una gran quantità di carta, portando enormi annunci che una Riunione Pubblica sarebbe stata tenuta alle ore una puntuale, per prendere in considerazione la convenienza di presentare una petizione al Parlamento a favore della United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking and Punctual Delivery Company, con capitale di cinque milioni, in cinquecentomila azioni da dieci sterline ciascuna; somme che erano debitamente esposte in grosse cifre nere di notevoli dimensioni. Il signor Bonney si fece strada con vigore su per le scale, ricevendo nel suo cammino molti inchini dai camerieri che si trovavano sui pianerottoli per indicare la strada; e, seguito dal signor Nickleby, si immerse in una serie di appartamenti dietro la grande sala pubblica: nel secondo dei quali c'era un tavolo dall'aspetto professionale e diverse persone dall'aria d'affari.

«Ascoltate!», gridò un signore con un mento [[topoi/double|doppio]], mentre il signor Bonney si presentava. «Sedetevi, signori, sedetevi!»

I nuovi arrivati furono accolti con unanime approvazione, e il signor Bonney si affrettò a salire in cima al tavolo, si tolse il cappello, si passò le dita tra i capelli e batté un colpo da cocchiere di piazza sul tavolo con un martelletto: a questo diversi signori gridarono «Sentite!» e si fecero un cenno a vicenda, come per dire che era proprio un comportamento pieno di spirito. Proprio in questo momento, un cameriere, febbrile per l'agitazione, irruppe nella sala, spalancò la porta con un tonfo e gridò «Sir Matthew Pupker!»

Il comitato si alzò in piedi e applaudì per la gioia, e mentre
applaudivano, entrò Sir Matthew Pupker, accompagnato da due membri
viventi del Parlamento, uno irlandese e uno scozzese, tutti sorridenti e
inchinandosi, e con un'aria così piacevole che sembrava un vero miracolo
che qualcuno potesse avere il coraggio di votare contro di loro. Sir
Matthew Pupker in particolare, che aveva una piccola testa rotonda con una
parrucca bionda sulla cima, cadde in un tale parossismo di inchini che
la parrucca minacciava di essere strappata via, ogni istante. Quando
questi sintomi si furono in qualche modo attenuati, i gentiluomini che
erano in rapporti di parola con Sir Matthew Pupker, o con i due altri
membri, si affollarono intorno a loro in tre piccoli gruppi, vicino a uno
dei quali i gentiluomini che NON erano in rapporti di parola con Sir
Matthew Pupker o con i due altri membri, si fermavano esitanti, sorridendo
e strofinandosi le mani, nella disperata [[concepts/hope|speranza]] che qualcosa
potesse capitare che li portasse all'attenzione. Tutto questo
[[motifs/time|tempo]], Sir Matthew Pupker e i due altri membri stavano raccontando
ai loro circoli separati quali fossero le intenzioni del governo
riguardo all'approvazione del disegno di legge; con un resoconto
dettagliato di ciò che il governo aveva detto sottovoce
l'ultima [[motifs/time|volta]] che avevano cenato con esso, e come il governo
fosse stato osservato strizzare l'occhio quando lo diceva; da cui
premesse non avevano difficoltà a trarre la conclusione che se il
governo aveva un obiettivo più a cuore di un altro, quell'obiettivo
era il benessere e il vantaggio della United Metropolitan Improved Hot
Muffin and Crumpet Baking and Punctual Delivery Company.

Nel frattempo, in attesa che si organizzassero le procedure e si distribuisse equamente il tempo di parola, il pubblico nella grande sala si divideva tra lo scrutare il palco vuoto e le signore in galleria. A questi passatempi la maggior parte di loro si era dedicata per un paio d'ore, e poiché anche le distrazioni più piacevoli finiscono per stancare se prolungate troppo a lungo, gli spiriti più intransigenti cominciarono a battere i piedi sul pavimento e a manifestare il loro malcontento con fischi e grida. Questi sforzi vocali, provenienti da coloro che erano lì da più tempo, naturalmente partivano da quelli più vicini al palco e più lontani dai poliziotti di servizio, i quali, non avendo grande voglia di farsi largo tra la folla, ma nutrendo nondimeno un lodevole [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di fare qualcosa per reprimere il disordine, si misero subito a trascinare fuori, per le code dei cappotti e i colletti, tutte le persone tranquille vicino alla porta; nello stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]] distribuivano vari colpi secchi e pungenti con i loro manganelli, secondo il metodo di quel geniale attore, il signor Punch: il cui brillante esempio, sia per quanto riguarda il tipo di armi che il loro uso, questa branca dell'esecutivo segue occasionalmente.

Erano in corso parecchi scontri molto accesi, quando un grido potente attirò l'attenzione anche dei belligeranti, e poi sulla piattaforma, da una porta laterale, si riversò una lunga fila di signori a cappello in mano, tutti che guardavano dietro di sé e lanciavano acclamazioni rumorose; la ragione di ciò fu sufficientemente spiegata quando Sir Matthew Pupker e gli altri due veri membri del Parlamento si fecero avanti, tra grida assordanti, e si dimostrarono l'un l'altro con gesti muti che non avevano mai visto una vista così gloriosa come quella, in tutto il corso della loro carriera pubblica.

Alla fine, e finalmente, l'assemblea smise di gridare, ma Sir Matthew Pupker, eletto presidente, subì una ricaduta che durò cinque minuti. Finito questo, Sir Matthew Pupker continuò a dire quali dovevano essere i suoi sentimenti in quella grande occasione, e quale doveva essere quell'occasione agli occhi del mondo, e quale doveva essere l'intelligenza dei suoi compatrioti davanti a lui, e quale doveva essere la ricchezza e la rispettabilità dei suoi onorevoli amici dietro di lui, e infine, quale doveva essere l'importanza per la ricchezza, la felicità, il comfort, la libertà, l'esistenza stessa di un popolo libero e grande, di un'Istituzione come la United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking and Punctual Delivery Company!



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_02--part_04" data-title="Nicholas Nickleby — Chapter 2 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 02" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="topos/double,archetype/orphan,motif/bells,motif/nature,motif/snow,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/despair,concept/doubt,concept/honour,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,setting/london,character/nicholas_nickleby,character/ralph_nickleby"></span>
